content_voiceover: This is the classic coagulation cascade diagram, the one every hematology fellow needs to know cold for boards. On the left, the intrinsic pathway begins with factor twelve, the Hageman factor, being activated by contact with negatively charged surfaces, working through prekallikrein and high molecular weight kininogen to activate factor eleven, then factor nine. On the right, the extrinsic pathway starts with tissue injury exposing tissue factor, which complexes with factor seven to form the tissue factor VIIa complex. Both pathways converge on factor ten, activating it to factor Xa, which is the start of the common pathway shown at the bottom. Factor Xa, together with factor Va, calcium, and a phospholipid surface, forms the prothrombinase complex that converts prothrombin, factor two, into thrombin, factor IIa. Thrombin then does double duty, it feeds back to activate factors five and eight as cofactors, and it cleaves fibrinogen into fibrin, which factor XIIIa then cross-links into a stable clot. Keep in mind this cascade model is a useful teaching framework, but it doesn't fully capture what happens in vivo, which we'll get to on the next slide.
keypoints: Intrinsic pathway: factor XII through XI, IX, activated by contact activation
Extrinsic pathway: tissue factor plus factor VII
Both converge at factor X to start the common pathway
Common pathway: Xa plus Va forms prothrombinase, generating thrombin
Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, cross-linked by factor XIII
keypoint_voiceover: Board tip. Intrinsic pathway is measured by PTT, extrinsic by PT, and both converge on the common pathway at factor Xa, ending in thrombin generation and cross-linked fibrin.
